# Results — Study 723 (Guacamole-Bowl): does the Super-Bowl guac binge print a Jan–Feb seasonal? 1993–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Tradable leg **PEP** (PepsiCo/Frito-Lay —
the Super-Bowl chip-and-dip complex; a **labelled proxy**, because the pure-play avocado name Calavo
`CVGW` is currently untradable on the Yahoo feed), benchmark **SPY**, cash leg **^IRX**, monthly
returns from daily closes resampled to month-end on a verified hole-free grid: 1993-02 → 2026-05,
**400 months**. As-of 2026-06-01; inputs fingerprint `14fdb930823d`. The wholesale-Hass avocado
seasonal is **hardcoded, cited, approximate** — shown for its shape only, never a Signal stamp.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `NONE` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Guacamole surge?" `BUSTED`

The folklore says America's Super-Bowl guacamole binge (early February) should print a January–February
seasonal in the avocado / produce trade. The tape says **the opposite**. The guac window (Jan–Feb)
*under*-performs the rest of the year by **−1.19%/month with t = −1.67** — the *wrong sign* — and a
placebo across all 66 month-pairs ranks Jan–Feb **9/66** (bottom 14%), one of the *weakest* windows of
the year, not one of the strongest. No calendar month clears |t| ≥ 2 in the window's favour (Jan
t_HAC = −0.36, Feb = +0.12); the only near-significant months (March t_HAC = +3.53, November = +2.30)
are off-thesis. A long-Jan–Feb timer earns **Sharpe −0.09** (−0.11 net) against buy-and-hold SPY's
**+0.61**. And the demand-price premise fails before the tape: the hardcoded wholesale-Hass seasonal
puts the guac window **5.9 index points below** the annual average — winter is the *soft* part of the
avocado price year. `NONE`, `MIRAGE`, surge `BUSTED`.

## Data stamp

- **Series**: PEP (tradable proxy) + SPY (benchmark) + ^IRX (cash) monthly, 1993-02 → 2026-05,
  **400 months**, as-of 2026-06-01, fingerprint `14fdb930823d`
- **Construction**: daily closes resampled to month-end (last close of each calendar month). Grid
  asserted hole-free on every read by `fetch_data`. PEP/SPY are auto-adjusted (total-return-ish),
  labelled as such; ^IRX is the 13-week T-bill rolled to a monthly cash return.
- **Avocado seasonal**: hardcoded 12-month wholesale-Hass price index (base 100 ≈ annual mean),
  reconstructed from public USDA AMS / Hass Avocado Board seasonality — **a labelled proxy, shape only**.
- **Proxy caveat**: the intended pure-play (Calavo, `CVGW`) returns a single bar on the current Yahoo
  feed, so the tradable leg is the strongest **available** expression of the Super-Bowl snack trade.

## Premise check — the avocado price's own seasonal shape

| month | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| seasonal index (100 = mean) | 95 | 97 | 100 | 103 | 102 | 105 | 110 | **114** | 111 | 103 | 93 | 90 |

Guac window (Jan–Feb) mean **96.0** vs annual mean **101.9** → **gap −5.9 index points**. The Super
Bowl is a *volume* event the supply chain pre-positions for; winter carries the heavy Mexican Hass
crop, so the marginal price is *soft*, and the real price peak is the late-summer supply gap (Aug).
The "price surge" premise is false before we look at a stock.

The two guac-window months are indistinguishable from zero (Jan is actually negative). The only
months near significance — March and November — have nothing to do with the Super Bowl and would not
survive Bonferroni for 12 tests (α = 0.05/12 ≈ 0.004 ⇒ |t| ≈ 3).

## The guac-window spread + the placebo (the headline)

| | Mean monthly return | n |
|---|---|---|
| Guac window (Jan–Feb) | −0.14% | 67 |
| Rest of year | +1.04% | 333 |
| **Spread (window − rest)** | **−1.19%** | — |
| **t-stat (Welch)** | **−1.67** | — |
| **Block-bootstrap 95% CI** | **[−2.61%, +0.26%]** | 5000 resamples, 12-month blocks |
| **Placebo rank among 66 month-pairs** | **9 / 66 (bottom 14%, z = −1.32)** | — |

The spread is the *wrong sign* and the placebo is decisive: of all 66 possible month-pairs, the
Super-Bowl window is in the bottom decile. The most *positive* pairs are all off-thesis (Mar–Oct
+2.14%/mo, Mar–Nov +1.47%, Oct–Nov +1.37%). **The guac window is not special — it's a laggard.**

## Calendar timer vs buy-and-hold

Long PEP in Jan–Feb, T-bill otherwise (calendar-known rule, no execution lag). Sharpe = excess of
T-bill, both legs. Net charges 5 bp one-way × NAV per leg (2 legs/yr).

| | CAGR | Sharpe (excess) | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|
| guac timer (gross) | +1.5% | **−0.09** | −30% |
| guac timer (net 5 bp/leg) | +1.4% | −0.11 | −31% |
| buy & hold PEP | +8.7% | +0.42 | −36% |
| buy & hold SPY | +10.9% | **+0.61** | −51% |

The timer holds the market only during its worst two months and earns cash the rest of the year, for a
**negative** Sharpe. Buy-and-hold SPY laps it. PEP's own alpha vs SPY is an insignificant **+3.46%/yr
(Newey-West t = +1.27, β = 0.59)** — no harvestable edge even ignoring the seasonal, and the wrong
instrument for an avocado thesis regardless.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic world with a *planted* +3%/mo Jan–Feb premium (seed 723): the engine recovers window
spread **+3.70%/mo, t = +4.60**, placebo rank **66/66** (the extreme tail), and a timer Sharpe **+0.65**
beating buy-and-hold **−0.16**. Under the null (premium 0) it finds spread +0.10%/mo, **t = +0.12** —
nothing. The harness can bank a real seasonal, so the flat, wrong-tail result on the real tape is a
true null, not a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The guac window under-performs the rest of the year by −1.19%/mo (t = −1.67, wrong
  sign); no thesis month clears |t| ≥ 2 in its favour; the placebo ranks Jan–Feb 9/66; the bootstrap CI
  [−2.61%, +0.26%] sits mostly below zero. There is no positive Super-Bowl seasonal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A long-Jan–Feb timer earns a *negative* Sharpe (−0.09 gross, −0.11 net) vs
  buy-and-hold SPY's +0.61; PEP carries no significant alpha (t = 1.27); and the on-thesis instrument
  (Calavo) is a thin micro-cap that isn't even reliably on the tape.
- **"Guacamole surge?" — BUSTED.** The avocado price is soft in winter (guac window 5.9 pts below the
  annual mean) and the snack tape's window is the year's weakest — both legs point the wrong way. The
  binge is a real, well-supplied *volume* event; there is no *price* left for a trader.

> **Caveat (named, not buried).** The avocado seasonal is a **small, hardcoded, approximate**
> reconstruction of public reporting — its *shape* is defensible, its precise values are not a live
> feed — and the tradable leg is a **labelled proxy** (PEP is the Super-Bowl snack complex, not an
> avocado, chosen because the pure-play CVGW is unavailable on the feed). Both limitations push the
> verdict toward humility, not toward a stronger claim: nothing here supports a guac seasonal, and
> several lines point the other way.
